difficultyReason: Two plainly juxtaposed facts — park expansion yet attendance decline — with one obvious confounder (a competing attraction) that explains the decline without contradicting the expansion.
stimulus: Last year, the town of Millbrook doubled the size of Riverside Park and added new playgrounds, picnic areas, and walking trails. Yet annual attendance at Riverside Park fell by nearly 30 percent compared with the previous year.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent paradox?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Riverside Park's budget for maintenance did not increase along with its size.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A large new amusement park opened five miles from Millbrook last year, drawing many of Riverside Park's former visitors.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The walking trails at Riverside Park are longer than any others in the region.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Millbrook's population has been growing steadily for the past decade.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Attendance at Riverside Park had been rising each year for the five years before the expansion.

explanations.correct: The expansion made the park more appealing, which should have raised attendance; the competing new amusement park siphoned visitors away. Both facts can be true at once once the alternative attraction is introduced.
explanations.A: Lower maintenance relative to size might hurt the park, but nothing in the stimulus suggests visitors noticed neglect — it doesn't explain the sharp drop.
explanations.C: Irrelevant — a superlative about the trails doesn't address why fewer people came.
explanations.D: Deepens the paradox — a growing population should have raised, not lowered, attendance at an expanded park.
explanations.E: Deepens the paradox — a rising trend before the expansion makes the post-expansion drop even more surprising.

difficultyReason: Hospital ER: more patients yet shorter waits. The obvious resolution is a large staffing increase that more than kept pace with the patient rise.
stimulus: St. Alban's Hospital reports that the number of patients arriving at its emergency room rose by 25 percent this year over last year. Nonetheless, the average time a patient waited before being seen by a physician fell from 45 minutes to 30 minutes during the same period.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent paradox?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most of the hospital's patients this year came from neighborhoods that are farther from the hospital than last year's patients were.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patients at the hospital have expressed higher satisfaction with their care this year than last year.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The hospital doubled the number of emergency-room physicians and nurses on duty at the start of this year.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The hospital's emergency room is now the only one operating in the county.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Last year's wait times at St. Alban's were longer than wait times at most other hospitals in the region.

explanations.correct: A 25 percent rise in patients should lengthen waits, but doubling the clinical staff dramatically increases throughput — enough to absorb the added demand and shorten waits overall.
explanations.A: Travel distance affects arrival, not in-hospital wait time after arrival.
explanations.B: Patient satisfaction is a consequence, not an explanation, of shorter waits.
explanations.D: Deepens the paradox — being the only ER in the county would concentrate demand and lengthen waits.
explanations.E: Comparison with other hospitals doesn't explain St. Alban's own year-over-year change.

difficultyReason: Local habitat destroyed yet species population rises — resolved by the single obvious fact that the birds relocated to a protected site.
stimulus: Biologists report that more than half of the marshland surrounding Lake Corren, the traditional nesting site of the yellow-throated tern, was drained for farmland during the past five years. Despite this, the regional population of yellow-throated terns increased by 15 percent over the same period.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent paradox?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The yellow-throated tern eats primarily small fish that are abundant in Lake Corren.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Farmland drained from marshes is usually less productive than farmland that was never marshland.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Five years ago a large, previously unknown wetland 20 miles from Lake Corren was designated a protected bird sanctuary, and most of the displaced terns nested there successfully.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The yellow-throated tern is closely related to several other tern species whose populations have declined.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Drainage of the marshland around Lake Corren has been more extensive than biologists initially predicted.

explanations.correct: The new protected wetland gave the displaced terns somewhere to go. Habitat was lost at Lake Corren, but equivalent habitat became available nearby — so regional numbers could still rise.
explanations.A: Food availability at the old site doesn't explain how the population grew after half that site was destroyed.
explanations.B: A fact about the farmland, not the terns — doesn't address the population figure.
explanations.D: Irrelevant — the paradox is about this species, not its relatives.
explanations.E: Deepens the paradox — more drainage should have harmed the population further.

difficultyReason: Fewer downloads yet higher revenue — resolved by a shift to higher-priced enterprise licenses. Single clear mechanism.
stimulus: Vortex Software reports that the total number of downloads of its flagship design program fell by 20 percent last year compared with the year before. Even so, Vortex's revenue from that program rose by 35 percent over the same period.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent paradox?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Last year Vortex began offering the program primarily to corporate customers through licenses that cost many times more than a single-user download.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vortex's main competitor released a similar program last year at a lower price.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most of Vortex's downloads last year came from first-time users rather than from returning customers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vortex's advertising budget was smaller last year than in the year before.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vortex's development costs for the program were higher last year than the year before.

explanations.correct: If each corporate license brings in many times what a single download does, a smaller number of high-value licenses can easily yield 35 percent more revenue than a larger number of low-value downloads.
explanations.B: Deepens the paradox — a cheaper competitor should have depressed Vortex's revenue, not raised it.
explanations.C: First-time versus returning users doesn't explain the revenue rise.
explanations.D: Smaller ad spend might explain fewer downloads but not higher revenue.
explanations.E: Costs don't determine revenue — this doesn't address the question.

difficultyReason: Museum attendance rises while gift-shop revenue falls — resolved by noting the new visitors came on free-admission days when spending is far lower.
stimulus: The Hartwell Museum of History reports that total annual visitors rose by 40 percent after it introduced a new free-admission day each month last year. However, revenue from the museum's gift shop fell by 10 percent during the same period.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent paradox?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nearly all of the museum's increased attendance came on the new free-admission days, and visitors on those days spend, on average, far less in the gift shop than paying visitors do.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The gift shop at the museum offers a wider variety of items than any comparable museum shop in the city.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most items in the museum's gift shop are priced higher than comparable items elsewhere.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Attendance at other history museums in the region rose last year as well.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The museum's overall operating budget was lower last year than the year before.

explanations.correct: If the extra visitors overwhelmingly came on free days and spend very little, then gift-shop revenue can fall even as attendance rises — the new crowd simply isn't buying.
explanations.B: A fact about product variety doesn't explain a revenue decline.
explanations.C: Higher prices could raise revenue per sale or deter sales — ambiguous, and it doesn't tie to the attendance surge.
explanations.D: Irrelevant — other museums' numbers don't explain Hartwell's shop revenue.
explanations.E: The budget doesn't determine how much visitors spend in the gift shop.

difficultyReason: Concert attendance up but ticket revenue down — one-step resolution via a deep ticket discount.
stimulus: The Bayside Symphony reports that attendance at its concerts rose by 50 percent this season over last season. Nevertheless, total ticket revenue for the season fell by 20 percent.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent paradox?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The symphony performed the same number of concerts this season as last season.

choices.label: B
choices.text: This season the symphony cut the price of every ticket by more than half in order to fill empty seats.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Attendance at competing orchestras in the region also rose this season.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The symphony's musicians received a modest pay raise at the start of this season.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reviews of this season's performances were on the whole more positive than last season's.

explanations.correct: Cutting every ticket's price by more than half while attendance rises only 50 percent means revenue per seat drops faster than seats sold rise. Total revenue can fall even as audiences grow.
explanations.A: Holding the number of concerts constant rules out one alternative explanation but doesn't itself explain lower revenue.
explanations.C: Other orchestras' attendance is irrelevant to Bayside's revenue.
explanations.D: Musician pay is a cost, not a revenue figure.
explanations.E: Better reviews would tend to raise ticket demand and revenue, if anything.

difficultyReason: Lower speed limit yet more fatalities — resolved by a sharp rise in traffic volume that overwhelms the per-driver safety gain.
stimulus: Three years ago, the state of Corinth lowered the speed limit on its rural highways from 65 to 55 miles per hour, expecting a reduction in traffic fatalities. Yet the total number of traffic fatalities on those highways has risen by 12 percent since the change took effect.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent paradox?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Drivers in Corinth have reported feeling safer on the highways since the speed-limit change.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some neighboring states have retained higher speed limits on their rural highways.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Since the speed-limit change, the total number of vehicles using Corinth's rural highways has more than doubled.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Police in Corinth have issued more speeding tickets each year since the change than they did before.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most fatal accidents on rural highways involve drivers who were unfamiliar with the route.

explanations.correct: Fatalities depend on both the per-mile risk and the number of miles driven. Doubling the traffic can produce more total deaths even when each trip is safer — so both facts can be true.
explanations.A: Feelings of safety don't bear on the actual fatality count.
explanations.B: Neighboring states' rules don't explain Corinth's own change.
explanations.D: More tickets suggests more speeding, which would deepen rather than resolve the paradox about a lower limit.
explanations.E: A general fact about fatal accidents doesn't explain why the count rose after the limit dropped.

difficultyReason: Printed-dictionary sales fall while word-lookup volume rises — resolved by noting lookups migrated to free online dictionaries.
stimulus: Sales of printed English dictionaries in the country of Lindoria have fallen by more than 60 percent over the past decade. However, surveys indicate that the total number of times Lindorians looked up the meaning of an English word rose substantially during that same decade.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent paradox?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most printed dictionaries sold in Lindoria are purchased as gifts rather than for personal use.

choices.label: B
choices.text: During the past decade, free online dictionaries have become widely available in Lindoria, and most word lookups there now take place on those sites.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lindorian schools have begun assigning fewer writing exercises than they did a decade ago.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Printed dictionaries now cost considerably more than they did ten years ago.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The average English vocabulary of an adult Lindorian has grown modestly over the past decade.

explanations.correct: If lookups simply moved from printed books to free online sites, Lindorians can look up more words overall while buying far fewer printed dictionaries. Both halves of the paradox are explained at once.
explanations.A: Gift-versus-personal use is orthogonal to whether lookups are happening elsewhere.
explanations.C: Fewer writing exercises would tend to lower lookups, deepening the paradox.
explanations.D: Higher prices help explain the sales drop alone but not why lookups rose.
explanations.E: A modest vocabulary rise doesn't by itself account for more lookups with fewer dictionaries.

difficultyReason: Fewer arrests yet more convictions — resolved by noting prosecutors now pursue only cases with stronger evidence, raising the conviction rate enough to offset fewer arrests.
stimulus: The Oakridge County district attorney reports that the number of arrests for burglary in the county fell by 30 percent last year compared with the year before. Even so, the number of burglary convictions obtained in the county's courts rose by 15 percent during the same period.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent paradox?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At the start of last year the district attorney's office adopted a policy of taking only burglary cases supported by strong physical evidence to trial, and the share of such cases ending in conviction has risen sharply.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oakridge County has the highest burglary rate of any county in the state.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Many of those arrested for burglary in previous years were repeat offenders.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Last year judges in Oakridge County imposed longer sentences for burglary than in any recent year.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Defense attorneys in Oakridge County are widely regarded as among the most effective in the state.

explanations.correct: When only strong-evidence cases go to trial, a much higher share convict. Even with fewer arrests feeding the pipeline, that higher conviction share can yield more total convictions.
explanations.B: A baseline rate doesn't explain a year-over-year change.
explanations.C: Repeat-offender status is a background fact; it doesn't address why convictions rose.
explanations.D: Sentence length is about punishment, not whether convictions occur.
explanations.E: Strong defense attorneys would tend to lower, not raise, conviction counts — deepening the paradox.

difficultyReason: Ethicists publicly endorse a principle yet privately decline to follow it — resolved by a single clear distinction between the principle they endorse and the one the situation would require.
stimulus: In a recent survey, 90 percent of professional ethicists publicly endorsed the principle that people have a strong duty to give substantial portions of their income to charity. Yet when asked about their own practice, nearly all of those same ethicists reported giving only a very small share of their income to charity.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent paradox?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most of the ethicists surveyed work at universities where salaries are lower than those in comparable professions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The principle that most of the ethicists endorsed applies, by its own terms, only to people whose income is many times higher than any of the surveyed ethicists earn.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Charities in the ethicists' communities have received less total funding this year than last year.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ethicists surveyed in previous years endorsed the same principle at a similar rate.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most people who donate to charity give without first consulting any ethical principle.

explanations.correct: If the endorsed principle by its own terms applies only to much higher earners, the ethicists' low giving is consistent with their endorsement — the duty they accept simply doesn't bind people at their income level.
explanations.A: Lower salaries might explain small gifts but not why the ethicists endorse a demanding duty they appear to ignore.
explanations.C: Community-wide funding totals don't address the ethicists' individual giving.
explanations.D: Historical endorsement rates don't reconcile the gap between words and deeds.
explanations.E: A claim about most donors doesn't speak to ethicists, who are defined by engaging with principles.
